strengths: Well-motivated problem: incorporating conditional mean and covariance priors into diffusion/flow-based probabilistic time series forecasting addresses a real gap (cross-variable correlations and heteroscedasticity neglected by prior-informed methods like TMDM and NsDiff).
The paper provides a unified framework (CW-Gen) under which existing prior-informed approaches (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) can be viewed as special cases, which is a useful conceptual contribution.

The conditional whitening operation is elegant: it is an invertible linear transformation that lets standard DDPM/flow matching training remain unchanged while making the effective terminal distribution better matched to the data, and the CW-Flow variant removes the need for matrix inversion.

The JMCE loss is derived from a concrete theoretical condition (Theorem 1), giving a principled connection between estimator accuracy and terminal KL divergence, and includes an eigenvalue regularization term for numerical stability.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 6 state-of-the-art generative models across 5 real-world datasets, 10 random seeds with standard deviations, multiple probabilistic metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, conditional FID, ProbMSE/MAE), plus qualitative illustrations and ablation studies; consistent win rates (~79-92%) for the CW variants.
The framework is model-agnostic and demonstrated to plug into diverse backbones (diffusion and flow matching), suggesting practical utility and reusability.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: mean regressors (CARD, TMDM) and variance regressors (NsDiff, TsFlow's GP priors) already exist; the core contribution is extending these to a full conditional covariance whitening, which is a natural but not surprising extension.

The theory-to-practice link is loose: Theorem 1 is only a sufficient condition on the KL divergence between the data and the terminal Gaussian; the claim that reducing this KLD improves sample quality relies on heuristic arguments citing diffusion estimation error bounds, and the actual connection to end-to-end generation quality is not formally established.

Some empirical gains are small or mixed, e.g., CW-TMDM and CW-NsDiff show marginal or slightly negative changes in CRPS on ETTh1, and improvements over the strongest prior-informed baseline (NsDiff) are modest, raising questions about how much benefit the covariance prior adds beyond existing mean/variance priors.

The evaluation is purely self-referential (Raw vs. CW of the same model); no comparison against other prior-informed mechanisms at equal capacity, and the recently related TsFlow is discussed but not empirically compared.
Distribution shift mitigation claims are supported only qualitatively (Figure 2 mean-shift observation) rather than with a controlled quantitative experiment or known shift benchmarks.

Missing details weaken reproducibility within the main text: sliding-window covariance target definitions, computation cost of JMCE, and how the sliding-window covariance is computed on-line are deferred to appendices; no code release is mentioned.

Several typos and sloppy writing ('trainning', 'flow chat', 'standrad', 'NSDiff' vs 'NsDiff' inconsistently), and the 'four evaluation metrics' phrasing in the conclusion conflicts with the six metrics reported.
Only five datasets and one fixed forecast horizon setting (168/192, except ILI); results on higher-dimensional or genuinely non-stationary streaming settings would strengthen claims of robustness.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem (probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting) and the proposed CW-Gen framework is clean and modular: the conditional whitening transformation is invertible and can be grafted onto six existing diffusion/flow models, which is a practically useful property.

There is an attempt at theory (Theorem 1 gives a sufficient condition under which replacing N(0,I) with an estimated Gaussian terminal distribution reduces KL divergence; Theorem 2 compares with TMDM and NsDiff), and the JMCE loss is explicitly motivated by this condition rather than being purely heuristic.
The empirical protocol is reasonably thorough in scale: five datasets, six generative backbones, six metrics, ten repetitions with standard deviations, plus ablations deferred to the appendix.
The writing in the body is generally readable and the preliminaries make the paper accessible.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core idea — subtract an estimated conditional mean and rescale by an estimated conditional standard deviation (or covariance) before running a diffusion model — is an incremental extension of existing prior-informed methods (CARD, TimeDiff, TMDM, NsDiff's variance regressor, TsFlow's GP-based mean and variance priors). Replacing a per-variable variance with a full sliding-window covariance via a Cholesky-style parameterization is a natural step, and the paper does not clearly distinguish its contribution from these close predecessors beyond the claim that prior methods 'can be viewed as special cases'.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 1 essentially bounds the KL divergence between an arbitrary distribution and two fitted Gaussians; the sufficient condition (3) follows from standard KL decompositions and matrix inequalities. Moreover, the claimed link 'smaller terminal KL ⇒ better sample quality' is only indirect, via cited TV bounds whose other factors (score estimation error, discretization error) are not controlled, so the paper does not actually establish an end-to-end guarantee for the generative model.

Evaluation design is biased toward the proposed method. The headline comparison is 'Raw vs. CW' of the same backbones, with win rates as a primary summary statistic; absolute comparisons against prior-informed state-of-the-art (TMDM, NsDiff) are under-emphasized. In Table 2, CW degrades several results (e.g., TimeDiff QICE 9.513→12.610, NSDiff CRPS 0.407→0.416), contradicting the 'consistently improves' claim in the abstract, and no rigorous statistical significance testing accompanies the win-rate claims.

The claimed mitigation of distribution shift is supported only by qualitative visual illustrations (Figure 2) rather than any quantitative distribution-shift protocol (e.g., train/test shift benchmarks, rolling-origin evaluation), so this central claim in the abstract is not adequately substantiated.

Methodological concerns are not fully addressed: the sliding-window covariance target with window 95 (15 for ILI) and the choice λmin=0.1, wEigen=50 appear to be fixed without sensitivity analysis; the CW-Flow formulation (context-dependent source distribution N(μ̂,Σ̂)) risks train/test mismatch and its benefit over CW-Diff beyond computational cost is unclear; the effect of accurate covariance estimation on high-dimensional datasets (d=137) is not separately analyzed.
No mention of code or artifact release, which limits reproducibility given the many model–dataset combinations and tuned hyperparameters.

Polish issues undermine confidence: typos ('trainning', 'flow chat', 'standrad deviation'), inconsistent terminology (CW-Flow also called 'Conditional Whitened Flow Model' in the conclusion), and imprecise statements such as the covariance 'diminishing linear correlations among features' argument.

Only a subset of results (ETTh1) appears in the main text, with most evidence deferred to appendices that are not part of the submission provided, making it difficult to verify the breadth of the empirical claims.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: replacing the standard Gaussian terminal distribution with a conditionally parameterized Gaussian (conditional whitening) is a simple, general, and invertible transformation that can be plugged into existing diffusion and flow matching models.

Theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 provides a sufficient condition under which the modified terminal distribution reduces the KL divergence to the data distribution, and the JMCE loss is explicitly derived to satisfy this condition, creating a coherent theory-to-design pipeline. Theorem 2 (Appendix C) situates the method relative to TMDM and NsDiff.

Thorough empirical evaluation: six state-of-the-art generative models across five real-world datasets, with 10 random seeds, standard deviations, six metrics, and clear win-rate reporting. The paired Raw-vs-CW comparison is a clean and convincing experimental design that isolates the effect of the proposed whitening.

The JMCE with Cholesky parameterization and minimum-eigenvalue regularization is a sensible and practically relevant design for stable covariance estimation, supported by ablation studies in the appendix.
Illustrative results (Figure 2) give qualitative evidence for the claimed benefits on non-stationarity and distribution shift, complementing the quantitative tables.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is relatively loose: Theorem 1 is only a sufficient condition on the KL divergence between the data distribution and the terminal Gaussian. The link between a smaller terminal KL and actual end-to-end sample quality depends on additional error terms (score approximation error, discretization, τmin early stopping) that are not analyzed, so the claim of 'improving sample quality' is stronger than what is established.

The sliding-window covariance used as the regression target is itself a crude empirical estimate; the paper does not discuss sensitivity to the window size (95, or 15 for ILI) or how estimation error in this target propagates into the generative model.

The relationship to existing normalization-based approaches, particularly RevIN (Kim et al., 2022, cited only in passing) and whitening/instance-norm variants, is not adequately discussed or empirically compared, so the marginal benefit over simple normalization baselines is unclear.

Some results are unfavorable to CW-Gen (e.g., CW worsens QICE for TimeDiff and CRPS for NsDiff on ETTh1), and the paper does not analyze when or why the method hurts, nor is statistical significance testing reported despite 10 repeats.

Writing quality issues: several typos ('trainning', 'flow chat', 'standrad'), inconsistent citations for NsDiff (Li et al., 2024 vs. Ye et al., 2025), and Table 1's 'win rate' framing against baselines is somewhat loosely defined relative to the Raw-vs-CW win rates used elsewhere.
Computational overhead of JMCE training and eigen-decomposition relative to the raw models is discussed only superficially; a cost-benefit analysis would strengthen the practical case.

It is not demonstrated that the JMCE prior alone (e.g., sampling directly from N(μ̂, Σ̂)) is a weak or strong baseline, making it hard to gauge how much of the improvement comes from the generative model versus the prior itself.

strengths: The paper presents a clean and unifying perspective: several existing prior-informed diffusion/flow forecasting methods (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff, TimeDiff) can be cast as special cases of replacing the terminal distribution with an estimated conditional Gaussian, which is a useful conceptual contribution.

There is genuine theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 gives an explicit sufficient condition (in terms of estimation errors of the conditional mean and covariance) under which replacing N(0, I) with the estimated conditional Gaussian reduces the terminal-distribution KLD, and the JMCE loss (Eq. 4) is explicitly derived from this condition rather than being an ad-hoc heuristic. Theorem 2 further delineates when the proposal beats TMDM/NsDiff. Proofs are provided and rely on standard but correctly applied matrix inequalities.

The experimental study is unusually thorough for this subfield: six state-of-the-art generative backbones, five datasets, six metrics, 10 seeds with standard deviations, ablations on the two regularization hyperparameters (Tables 9-10), backbone choices (Table 11), sliding-window length (Tables 15-16), prior composition (Table 14), an end-to-end training variant (Table 18), comparison against univariate prior methods DSPD/TsFlow (Table 17), and honest reporting of computational cost including the O(d^3) bottleneck and a triangular-inverse acceleration (Tables 19-20).

The proposed CW transformation (whitening by the estimated covariance) is simple, invertible, and plugs into arbitrary diffusion and flow-matching models with essentially no architectural changes, which makes the contribution broadly applicable within probabilistic time series forecasting.
A reproducibility statement is included with code release, full algorithmic detail (Algorithms 1-7), and implementation specifics, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core mechanism—centering by a predicted mean and rescaling by a predicted (co)variance before applying a generative model—is conceptually close to instance/distribution normalization (RevIN, Non-stationary Transformers) and to the mean/variance regression priors of CARD, TimeDiff, and NsDiff. The novelty lies mainly in moving from diagonal variance to full sliding-window covariance and in the theoretical framing; some reviewers may view the contribution as incremental over NsDiff (Ye et al., 2025).

The theory provides only sufficient conditions involving unobservable population quantities (true conditional mean/covariance). The paper does not verify empirically that condition (3) actually holds on the evaluated datasets; the LHS proxy (Eq. 12) is reported in ablations but never connected back to the main results. Thus the theory justifies the loss design more than it guarantees the claimed sample-quality improvement.

The comparison protocol primarily contrasts each model against its own CW variant. While win rates are consistently favorable, absolute comparisons across models raise questions: several Raw baselines perform poorly relative to numbers reported in their original papers (e.g., TimeDiff and Diffusion-TS CRPS on ETTh2), suggesting possible under-tuning of baselines, and the CW numbers for some models (e.g., CW-TimeDiff) appear to roughly match well-tuned simple baselines. A comparison to a trivial 'prior-only' Gaussian sampler or RevIN-style normalization baseline is missing, which would clarify how much the full generative model contributes beyond the JMCE prior itself.

Scalability is a real limitation: eigen-decompositions with O(d^3) cost make the method expensive for high-dimensional data (Solar Energy shows mixed results and large overheads), and the proposed remedies either sacrifice the theoretical guarantees (diagonal covariance) or only partially mitigate the cost.

The claimed mitigation of 'distribution shift' is supported mainly by qualitative visualizations (Figure 2) rather than a controlled experiment (e.g., explicit train/test shift); the mechanism is essentially regression-based normalization, so the shift-robustness claim is somewhat stronger than the evidence.

Conditional FID depends on a specific TS2Vec embedding, and ILI is a very small dataset (966 points) with a 15-step window; robustness of conclusions on small-data regimes is less certain, as also acknowledged in the sliding-window ablation.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the proposed CW transformation is applied to six generative backbones across five standard time series datasets with 10 repetitions and standard deviations, which is more thorough than typical papers in this area.
Extensive ablation studies (hyperparameters of the eigenvalue penalty, sliding-window length, backbone choice, end-to-end training, individual prior components) are provided in the appendix.

The paper is clearly written, with a clean unified formulation (CW-Diff and CW-Flow) that shows prior methods such as CARD/TMDM and NsDiff-style variance priors are special cases of conditioning the terminal distribution.

The idea of jointly estimating a conditional mean and full sliding-window covariance, with an eigenvalue-regularization penalty, is sensible and practically motivated for non-stationary, heteroscedastic multivariate series.
Reproducibility statement, algorithms for all training/sampling routines, and released code support replication.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea amounts to applying a per-condition affine whitening transformation (mean centering plus covariance decorrelation) before a standard diffusion/flow model, then inverting it. This is a direct extension of well-known normalization techniques (e.g., reversible instance normalization, Kim et al. 2022) and of existing prior-informed diffusion models (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) from diagonal variance to full covariance. The delta over NsDiff in particular is incremental.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are direct consequences of the closed-form Gaussian KL decomposition (Lemma 1, already in Cardoso 2003) plus standard norm inequalities. The resulting sufficient condition involves unknown population quantities (true mean, covariance, estimation errors) that cannot be checked in practice, and no gap between the sufficient condition and actual generation quality is characterized. The claimed link to TV error bounds via prior work is loose and does not yield an end-to-end guarantee for CW-Diff.

The theory-practice connection is weak: the JMCE loss is 'designed to ensure (3) holds', but (3) can never be verified since it depends on the unknown true conditional moments; the appendix (Section D) essentially concedes the condition may fail in unfavorable regimes. Thus the theory serves mostly as post-hoc justification rather than a design guarantee.

Missing important baselines: the evaluation compares each model against its own CW variant, but does not compare against simpler, cheaper normalization schemes applied to the same backbones, such as per-window standardization, RevIN, or non-stationary normalization already built into some backbones. Without these, it is unclear how much of the gain comes specifically from the learned conditional covariance versus generic normalization.

Results are mixed in places: CW sometimes degrades performance (e.g., QICE on ILI and Solar, ProbCorr on Solar for several models, ProbMSE/ProbMAE on Solar), and the paper does not provide a principled explanation or a criterion for when whitening helps versus hurts, despite the theory purporting to characterize exactly this.

The very large Conditional FID reductions (often 5-10x) are somewhat suspicious and highly dependent on the TST2Vec encoder; given that the whitening transformation itself changes the marginal statistics, the improvement may partly reflect encoder sensitivity rather than genuine distributional fidelity.

Scalability concerns: the method requires per-time-step d x d covariance estimates and O(d^3) eigen-decompositions; on the 137-dimensional Solar dataset it is already slow (Table 20 shows ~60% overhead), and the proposed remedies (diagonal-only covariance) are acknowledged to break the theoretical motivation.
The statistical significance of the improvements is not assessed; with 10 runs and sometimes small margins, win-rate reporting without significance tests overstates the consistency of the gains.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: a unified 'conditional whitening' framework (CW-Gen) that incorporates conditional mean and covariance priors into both diffusion and flow-matching generative models, with prior methods (CARD/TMDM/NsDiff) shown as special cases.

Theoretical grounding is a genuine attempt at rigor: Theorem 1 gives a sufficient condition (in terms of KLD between the data and the terminal distribution) under which replacing N(0, I) with an estimated Gaussian prior helps, and Theorem 2 formally delineates when the proposed replacement improves over TMDM and NsDiff. The proofs in Appendix C appear largely correct (Pythagorean KLD decomposition, von Neumann trace inequality, terminal-distribution derivation for the SDE).

JMCE is a sensible design: Cholesky parameterization guarantees PSD covariance, and the eigenvalue penalty (L_min, w_Eigen) directly targets the inverse-min-eigenvalue term in the sufficient condition, with ablations (Tables 9-13) showing the penalty behaves as intended.

Unusually thorough empirical evaluation: six generative models integrated with the framework, five real datasets, 10 random seeds with standard deviations, consistent win rates (e.g., 83-100% on ETTh1/ETTh2), plus ablations on sliding-window length, JMCE backbones, component contributions (mean/var/cov), an end-to-end training variant, and computational cost analysis (Tables 15-21).
Comparisons beyond the six backbone models to DSPD and TsFlow (Table 17), and honest reporting of mixed cases (e.g., Solar Energy point-forecasting metrics, some QICE regressions).
Practical efficiency analysis with a triangular-inverse acceleration avoiding O(d^3) eigen-decomposition at sampling time (Appendix E.9), plus end-to-end training option.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate. The core idea — center and whiten the data by a predicted conditional mean/covariance before applying a standard generative model — is a fairly natural extension of the CARD/TMDM (mean-only) and NsDiff (diagonal variance) line of work; the main increment is a full-covariance prior plus eigenvalue regularization. The 'for the first time' claims should be tempered.

The sufficient condition in Theorem 1 involves unknown true quantities (the conditional mean and covariance and their estimation errors), so it is not directly verifiable in practice; the paper only checks a sample-surrogate 'LHS' metric (Eq. 12). The theory is thus more motivational than actionable, and the loss (4) only heuristically mirrors the condition.

The training target is the sliding-window covariance rather than the true conditional covariance; this gap is acknowledged but not quantified, and there is no analysis of when sliding-window covariance is a consistent/appropriate surrogate.

Results are not uniformly positive: on Solar Energy, point-forecast metrics (ProbMSE/ProbMAE) degrade for most CW variants (Tables 7-8, 50% win rate), several QICE results worsen (e.g., TimeDiff/SSSD on ILI and Weather), and improvements over the strongest baseline (NsDiff CW vs. Raw) are sometimes marginal. Some reported standard deviations look erroneous (e.g., negative values like '(0-467)' in Table 7, stds larger than means in Table 14), which suggests formatting/quality-control issues.

Two-stage training (JMCE then generative model) introduces error propagation; the end-to-end variant improves only some metrics and slightly worsens QICE, so the pipeline design is not fully resolved.

Scalability: O(d^3) eigen-decomposition of per-step covariance matrices makes the approach costly for high-dimensional series (Solar Energy takes ~14,460s of whitening alone), and the proposed mitigations (diagonal covariance) sacrifice the theory and performance.

Some exposition issues: the win-rate metric in Table 1 aggregates 24 comparisons in a way that can overstate consistency; Figure 1 caption contains a typo ('flow chat'); Theorem 1's statement is dense and its practical interpretation would benefit from being moved/discussed more carefully.
